title: Resolve a real merge conflict
summary: Two branches edit the same line. Git stops, marks the file, and waits for a human. Read the markers, resolve them properly, and finish the merge.
mental_model: A conflict is not an error. Git is saying: two people changed the same line and I refuse to guess which one is right. It hands you the file with both versions marked and pauses the merge until you commit a resolution.
danger: Never resolve a conflict by deleting the half you do not understand. Read both sides, then write the line that is actually correct — often that is neither side verbatim.

write.content:
tank:
  name: reef-01
  target_temp_c: 25.0
  ph: 8.1
  pump_rpm: 1200

tank:
  name: reef-01
  target_temp_c: 26.5
  ph: 8.1
  pump_rpm: 1200

commit.message: Raise target temperature for coral growth

write.content:
tank:
  name: reef-01
  target_temp_c: 24.0
  ph: 8.1
  pump_rpm: 1600

commit.message: Lower temperature and raise pump speed

steps.title: See the two histories before merging
steps.why: Both branches changed target_temp_c from the same starting value. The merge base is the commit they share. A three-way merge compares base-to-ours and base-to-theirs; overlapping edits become a conflict.

steps.title: Trigger the conflict
steps.why: The merge stops halfway. Git has already merged the non-overlapping parts and left the file with markers where it could not decide. The repo is now in a MERGE_IN_PROGRESS state — look at the badge on the right.
steps.expect: CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.yaml — exit code 1 is normal here.

steps.title: Read the markers instead of fearing them
steps.why: `<<<<<<< HEAD` starts your side, `=======` splits, `>>>>>>> feature/warmer` ends their side. The pump_rpm line merged cleanly on its own — only the contested line is marked.

steps.title: See each side on its own
steps.why: During a conflict git keeps three versions in the index: stage 1 base, stage 2 ours, stage 3 theirs. These commands print them without you having to untangle the markers by eye.

steps.title: Resolve it — with a value neither side wrote
steps.why: The correct answer here is a compromise: 26.0. This is the point people miss — resolution means writing the right code, not picking a team. (Click config.yaml on the right to edit it yourself instead of using this button.)

write.content:
tank:
  name: reef-01
  target_temp_c: 26.0
  ph: 8.1
  pump_rpm: 1600

verify.label: no conflicted files remain
verify.hint: fix the markers, then git add config.yaml

steps.title: Finish the merge
steps.why: `git add` was you telling git the conflict is settled. The commit seals it, with two parents. Until you commit, `git merge --abort` would still put everything back exactly as it was.

verify.label: working tree is clean — the merge is finished
verify.hint: git add the resolved file, then git commit

verify.label: no conflict markers were left in the file
verify.hint: this is the classic production incident: markers committed into a config file

verify.label: HEAD is the merge commit, with both branches as parents
the non-conflicting change from main survived
verify.hint: resolving must not throw away the parts git merged cleanly

pitfalls: Committing conflict markers is one of the most common real outages — a YAML file with `<<<<<<<` in it fails to parse at deploy time.
`git checkout --ours <file>` takes your whole side of the file, not just the conflicted line. It is a blunt instrument.
`git merge --abort` is safe and complete until you commit. Reach for it when you are lost.
Enable `git config rerere.enabled true` and git remembers how you resolved a conflict, replaying it if the same one appears again.
cheatsheet: your side; :3: is theirs, :1: is the shared base
take your whole version of the file
put everything back the way it was
